September 2036. Elena has come to Berlin for two months. On 25 October she's taking the Goethe B2 exam. Today she's doing her first practice test in the Leseecke. Elif is keeping time.
No! I'm only on part three. I read every text word for word.
That's the problem. In part one you only need to know who thinks what. Reading for the gist is enough there.
But if I don't understand a word, I can't read on. It's like a pothole in the road.
Then go round it. Like Leo with the tram. You don't have to know every word. You just have to know where the sentence is heading.
And how do I know that?
From the signal words. “Aber”, “jedoch”, “im Gegenteil”. If it says “aber”, the important opinion usually comes after it.
And in part two? There, for three questions, I found the word from the question in the text and ticked it. All wrong.
That's the trap. If the same word is in the text, it's often the wrong answer. The right one is usually said in other words.
You're twelve and you sound like an examiner.
Twelve since July. And I wrote Frau Hoffmann's whole book. I know how texts work.

“nicht unbedingt” = not necessarily; “kaum” = hardly, barely. These little words completely change the meaning of a sentence.

1) The same word in the text and in the option — often a trap; the right answer uses synonyms. 2) The option says “too much” — the text says “manche” (some), the option says “alle” (all). 3) The option is true in general, but the text doesn't say it. 4) Hidden negatives: kaum, selten, keineswegs.
Elimination strategy: first cross out the options that are definitely wrong. If two are left, look in the text for the word that makes the difference.

Elena Ionescu arrived on Monday, the fifteenth of September two thousand and thirty-six, on the night train from Budapest to Berlin, with a big suitcase full of textbooks, a small suitcase full of clothes and a jar of honey for every person she knew in Berlin, which by now meant, as Dan had remarked while she was packing, “more jars than clothes”. She was to stay ten weeks, in Lena and Andrei's spare room on the first floor of number thirty-one, and on Saturday, the twenty-fifth of October, take the exam for the Goethe B2 certificate at the Goethe-Institut on Neue Schönhauser Straße. She had been learning German for five years. She had started when Andrei decided to stay in Berlin, “so that I understand my son when he ends up dreaming only in German”. Now she wanted it in writing. With a stamp.

Her German was good. She spoke fluently, with the Transylvanian accent Ludwig liked so much, and understood almost everything as long as people didn't speak too fast. But she had a habit which, as Elif noticed on the very first day, was “deadly in an exam”: she read every word. Every single one. When she didn't know a word, she stopped, looked it up in the dictionary, wrote it in a little notebook, with the Romanian translation and an example sentence, and only then read on. That was how she had learnt for five years, and that was how she had collected, as she proudly told them, eight thousand four hundred words, in eleven notebooks, all carefully numbered. “That's wonderful,” said Elif. “And in the exam you have sixty-five minutes for five texts. With your system you'll manage two.”

Elif becoming Elena's teacher hadn't been planned. Actually, Ludwig had offered to study with her, Katrin Krüger had offered to explain newspaper articles to her, and Lena had looked for a course at the adult education centre. But on the first evening, at dinner in the courtyard, Elif had picked up Elena's sample test, the practice book from the Goethe-Institut, leafed through it and then said: “It's like a puzzle. Can I join in?” And Elena, who had studied alone for five years, in the evenings, after work, at the kitchen table in Sibiu, with nobody to tell her whether she was doing it right, looked at the twelve-year-old girl and said: “Yes. Please.”

They studied in the Leseecke, in the cellar of number thirty-three, every afternoon at four, when Elif got back from school. Elif had a stopwatch she had borrowed from Leo, the old stopwatch from his training, with which he had once measured braking distances, and she took her job very seriously. The first practice test was, as Elena admitted later, “a disaster foretold”. After sixty-five minutes she was on part three. She hadn't even seen parts four and five. And of the tasks she had done, almost half were wrong, not because she hadn't understood the texts but, as Elif found when marking them, “because you read too well”.

“Too well?” asked Elena. Elif explained, with a patience that, as she said, she had learnt from Grete. In part two, a newspaper article about urban gardens in Berlin, Elena had looked, for three questions, for exactly the word in the text that was also in the answer, and then ticked that answer. “Gemeinschaftsgärten” (community gardens) in the question, “Gemeinschaftsgärten” in the text, so correct. But it was wrong, all three times. Because the correct answer was in the text in other words. “The examiners aren't stupid,” said Elif. “They know people look for identical words. That's why they set traps. When you find the same word, you have to be especially suspicious. Like with a man who says too often that he's honest.”

Elena laughed, but she understood. And in the following weeks she learnt what Elif called “Straßenbahnlesen” (tram reading), after Leo. You don't stop at every stop. You know where you want to go and only stop where it's necessary. In part one, the four opinions, she now read only the beginnings and the ends and looked for the words that worked like points on a track: “aber”, “jedoch”, “im Gegensatz dazu”. Because after a set of points, Elif said, the sentence goes in a different direction, and usually it's this other direction that counts. “Zwar finde ich Stadtgärten schön, aber …” (Admittedly I find urban gardens nice, but …) — and everything that came after the “aber” was the real opinion. Everything before it was just politeness.

Hotte of course had an opinion on this too. For forty years, as he told them, he had read the newspaper at the depot every morning, during his break, in twelve minutes, “and not every word, mind, just what's true”. In the GDR, he explained, you had to learn to read between the lines, because the important thing was never in the lines. “When the paper said: the supply of tropical fruit is essentially secured, that meant: there ain't no bananas.” He tapped Elena's sample test with his finger. “The word «im Wesentlichen» is like «zwar». There's always an «aber» after it, even if it ain't written.” Elena wrote “im Wesentlichen” in the twelfth notebook, which she had started secretly, although Elif wasn't allowed to know.

The hardest thing was leaving the notebooks alone. Elena had brought the eleven notebooks with the eight thousand four hundred words to Berlin, in the big suitcase, and wanted to look up every unknown word straight away. Elif forbade it. Not entirely: she was allowed to write the words down, but only after the test, not during it. During the test, Elena had to guess. From the context. From word formation, as in the chapter on adjectives, which she had revised with Ludwig: “unverzichtbar” — un-, verzichten, -bar — so something you can't do without. “Like honey,” said Elena. “Like honey,” Elif confirmed, and wrote it in the margin.

One Wednesday, Elif took Elena to the care home, to Grete, who by now stayed almost entirely in bed but insisted every Wednesday that Elif play for her, even if only for ten minutes. That Wednesday Elif didn't play. She read. Elena read Grete a page from the sample test, a text about music schools, slowly, with her Transylvanian accent, and Grete listened with her eyes closed. When Elena had finished, Grete opened her eyes. “In nineteen fifty-five,” she whispered, “I had my entrance exam for the conservatory. I had to sight-read. A piece I had never seen. I started reading every note, and after four bars I was lost. Then I stopped reading and started listening. The piece in my head. Where it wants to go.” She smiled faintly. “It's the same with texts. Listen to where they want to go. The notes come by themselves after that.”

Ludwig helped in his own way. Every evening at dinner he gave Elena a text to read and then asked her just one question, but only after she had finished reading, so that she didn't know what to pay attention to. That, he said, was the best exercise for global reading: you read to understand, not to search. The texts were stories from his own book. Elena read the story about the tram and the twelve books and answered the question “Why did Ludwig stop?” with a single word: “Love.” Ludwig said that was correct, but that in the exam she would need at least a whole sentence. Elena answered: “Because it was love at first sight, although actually it was second sight, because he had had the first one at the concert.” Ludwig was so impressed that he noted the sentence down for the next print run.

Lena watched all this from the kitchen, in the evenings, when her mother-in-law came back with red cheeks from studying, her notebook under her arm, and talked at dinner about signal words and traps the way other people talk about football matches. Until then Lena had known Elena as a quiet, serious woman who sewed embroidery in Sibiu, put honey in jars and said little about herself. In Berlin she was different. She laughed loudly, argued with Hotte about grammar, went to the theatre on her own and came back at midnight, excited, because she had understood “at least seventy per cent”. “I think,” Andrei said quietly to Lena one evening, “that Mum didn't study for five years for an exam. She studied for this. For these ten weeks.”

In the middle of October, Elena did her last practice test. Elif sat opposite her, with Leo's stopwatch, and Katrin Krüger, who had come back early from the newsroom that day, sat in the corner and marked in parallel, so as to be, as she said, “objective”. Elena read. She no longer read every word. She read the tasks first, underlined the key words, looked for the right place in the text, read carefully there, twice, and then ticked. At words she didn't know, she made a little dot in the margin and read on. After fifty-two minutes she put down her pen. Done. With thirteen minutes to spare, which she used to transfer her answers carefully onto the answer sheet and then check the hardest questions once more.

Katrin and Elif counted at the same time. Then they looked at each other. Then they counted again. Twenty-seven out of thirty. Ninety per cent. Elena sat completely still and looked at her hands. Then she stood up, without a word, climbed the cellar stairs, crossed the courtyard into the café, where Lena was just wiping the tables, and pulled the cord of the brass bell. Once. Loudly. It was just after four, the felt was lifted, and Dr Vogt, who was sleeping upstairs, would say later that it woke him and that, for the first time, he didn't feel disturbed but smiled, because from the way it rang he could hear that someone had achieved something.

In the evening, Elena called Dan in Sibiu on video and held the result up to the camera, the sheet with Elif's red writing: “27/30. Very good. Stop reading every word!” Dan looked at the screen for a long time. Then he disappeared for a moment and came back with something he held up to the camera: a small, old, worn notebook, held together with an elastic band. “My first German notebook,” he said in Romanian. “From nineteen eighty-eight. Back then I meant to learn German so I could talk to the Saxons in the village. I got as far as page four.” He opened it. On page four, in his young, clumsy handwriting, it said: “Ich heiße Dan. Ich bin Imker. Ich lerne Deutsch.” Below that there was nothing. Elena laughed and cried at the same time. “I'll write page five for you,” she said. “On the twenty-fifth of October.”

After the call, Elena sat alone in the kitchen on the first floor for a long time, with the twelfth notebook in front of her, the secret one. She leafed through it. There were only twenty-three words in it, not eight thousand, but she had learnt every one of them in Berlin, not from a book but from a person: “im Wesentlichen” from Hotte, “unverzichtbar” from Elif, “Straßenbahnlesen” from nobody, because the word didn't even exist, except on Kastanienallee. On the last page she wrote, in her neat handwriting, a single sentence, in German, without looking anything up: “Man muss nicht jedes Wort kennen, um zu verstehen, wohin ein Mensch will.” (You don't have to know every word to understand where a person wants to go.) Then she closed the notebook and went to bed, and for the first time in weeks she didn't dream of exam questions but of bees buzzing in German.
